name: Jaw contouring makeup (contour/highlight)
lead: Jaw contouring is the use of makeup shading and highlighting to make the jawline look sharper and more defined. A shade slightly darker than the skin is placed along and beneath the jaw to suggest shadow, a lighter shade is placed where the edge should catch light, and the two are blended so the lower face reads as more angular and the chin and neck separate more cleanly in photos and in person.[1][2]

The technique applies the general practice of contouring, in which darker shades recede and lighter ones advance. Contouring has a long theatrical and film history and became mainstream in the 2010s through celebrity and social media use.[1] It is temporary and cosmetic: the effect lasts until the makeup is removed, and it works as an optical illusion rather than changing bone or soft-tissue structure.

Brands and makeup artists present jaw contouring for both women and men. Men's grooming coverage in 2026 describes growing use of complexion products by straight men, with industry voices stressing subtle enhancement rather than heavy contouring.[3] Looksmaxxing forum threads discuss bronzer and contour as ways to change how a face is perceived without surgery.[4]

chain: Darker shade placed along and under the jaw
Lighter shade on the edge adds contrast
Jaw and chin look sharper and more defined
angle.text: People use jaw contouring to make the jawline look more angular and the face appear slimmer and more sculpted, for photos, events or everyday wear. The change is visual and lasts while the makeup is on.

infobox: Contour and highlight powders, creams or sticks; bronzer

paras: General contouring places a darker shade in hollows or along edges to suggest shadow and a lighter shade on prominent areas; strobing uses lighter shades only.[1] Applied to the jaw, the same shading principle is used to suggest a sharper edge.

A beauty brand tutorial describes tilting the chin up, applying a medium-dark contour along the edge of the jaw, adding a second layer under the chin and along the jaw for depth, blending with a clean brush into the chin and cheekbones, and finishing with a highlighter along the jawline for contrast while avoiding the chin. The tutorial states the aim as a sculpted jawline that appears slimmer and more chiselled.[2] Cream products give a more emphasized look than powder, and setting spray is used to hold the result.[1][2]

Men's makeup coverage describes the aim as looking more defined and well-rested rather than visibly made up, and industry figures quoted in that coverage describe the growth as being in subtle products.[3]

Wikipedia's general description of contouring uses a shade one or two tones darker than the skin, warm or cool, in hollows and along edges, and a shade one or two tones lighter on prominent areas; strobing uses little or no darker shading.[1] Powder products are often sold in palettes pairing a light and a dark shade, while cream and stick formats give a stronger effect and are usually blended with a brush or sponge.[1][2] For the jaw, practitioners generally think in terms of where the face meets the neck: shading below the jaw edge deepens the shadow there, and a light line on the edge makes the angle read more sharply, which is the optical basis of the technique.[2]

The Charlotte Tilbury tutorial lays the steps out in sequence: skincare and an SPF primer, then primer, colour corrector, foundation and concealer as a base, then contour along the jaw edge and under the chin, blending, highlight, and setting spray. It names a cream or liquid contour as the main product and a powder bronzer as an alternative, and lists a facial massage tool such as a gua sha as an optional extra.[2]

Elizabethan actors used chalk and soot so that expressions could be read from a distance, and greasepaint replaced soot once electric stage lighting arrived. Marlene Dietrich used shading in 1920s and 1930s films, and Max Factor Sr. added shading in 1934 so faces would not look flat on screen.[1] In 1945 Max Factor Sr. presented what Wikipedia describes as the first tutorial on contouring for different face shapes.[1] In the 1950s, actresses including Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe and Elizabeth Taylor are described as using subtle contouring and shading.[1]

Kevyn Aucoin (1962-2002) was an American make-up artist whose 1986 Vogue cover work with Cindy Crawford raised his profile; he became one of the best-paid celebrity makeup artists of his time and worked with celebrities such as Cher and Madonna.[6][1] His books include The Art of Makeup (1994), Making Faces (1999, a Time bestseller) and Face Forward (October 2000), which is credited with introducing makeup sculpting and contouring to the general public.[6][1]

In the 2010s, Kim Kardashian and other makeup artists intensified the trend, and affordable brands made contour and strobing products widely available. Drag performers use contouring to emphasize or soften features.[1]

Powder contour palettes usually pair a lighter and a darker shade, while cream, liquid and stick formats give a more emphasized result and are generally blended with a brush or sponge.[1][2] A powder bronzer is sometimes used in place of a dedicated contour shade.[2]

Strobing is the related approach that uses lighter shades and little or no darker shading.[1] On the jaw, makeup artists combine a shadow below the jaw edge with a light line on the edge itself, so that the angle between face and neck reads more sharply.[2] Body contouring applies the same shading principle to other areas such as shins or the chest.[1]

A looksmax.org thread titled around changing the entire face with bronzer, contour and fake tan reflects how some members treat makeup and tanning as quick tools for altering facial appearance.[4] Contouring is also discussed alongside non-temporary options such as jaw fillers and implants, which change real structure instead of shading it.

Whether contouring changes how a person is perceived is a recurring question in these communities. The looksmax.org thread title reflects the view that shading and fake tan together can alter the apparent face in photos.[4] Wikipedia's account of contouring places the technique in the world of photography, film and stage, where lighting and shading have long been used to alter how facial structure reads.[1]

Contouring entered mass culture in the 2010s through celebrity makeup artists and social media tutorials, with Kim Kardashian often credited with intensifying the trend, and affordable brands sold contour kits widely.[1] Wikipedia also notes that drag performers use contouring to emphasise or soften features.[1]

Men's makeup is a growing part of the grooming category. A February 2026 Personal Care Insights article quoted Jake Xu, co-founder of the men's beauty brand Shakeup Cosmetics, saying the growth is in tinted moisturisers, concealers and under-eye products to reduce redness and shine and brighten tired eyes. Xu said: "The growth we're seeing isn't about heavy contouring."[3] He described men's makeup as very niche about five years earlier and now part of the wider men's grooming section at retailers, and said the word "makeup" can still feel loaded for some customers.[3]
No studies found. A 2025 randomized trial compared facial roller and gua sha massage for facial contour, muscle tone and skin elasticity, which is a different intervention from makeup.[5]

lore.intro: Looksmax.org members discuss contour and bronzer as quick, non-surgical ways to change how the face looks in photos, while brand and trade coverage frames jaw contouring as shading for definition.[4][2][3]

claims.claim: Bronzer and contour can change how the whole face looks
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title states that you can pretty much change your entire face with bronzer, contour and fake tan.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes contouring as using shade and highlight to shape and enhance facial structure, and notes it has been used on film and stage for roughly a century.[1] No studies have measured jawline-specific effects.

claims.claim: Shading under and along the jaw makes it look sharper and slimmer
claims.believers: A beauty brand tutorial describes darker shade along the jaw edge and under the chin plus a highlighter on the edge as producing a sculpted, slimmer, more chiselled jawline.[2]
claims.experts: Wikipedia explains contouring as darker shades suggesting shadow and lighter shades suggesting prominence; it does not report jaw-specific measurements.[1] No published study has tested jaw contouring on perceived attractiveness.

claims.claim: Men's use of makeup is moving toward subtle, undetectable products
claims.believers: Shakeup Cosmetics co-founder Jake Xu told Personal Care Insights the growth is in tinted moisturisers, concealers and under-eye products, not heavy contouring.[3]
claims.experts: This is an industry observation from trade coverage rather than a research finding; no survey data on male jaw-contour use was located.[3]

card.summary: Shading and highlighting to fake a sharper jawline; temporary and cosmetic.
card.note: Cosmetic illusion only; no studies of jawline-specific effects found.

quick.overview:
Jaw contouring uses darker and lighter makeup to suggest a more defined jaw. It is the same shading idea used for cheekbones and noses.

It is temporary and works as an optical effect.
quick.mechanism: Darker shades read as shadow and lighter shades as raised areas, changing perceived shape.
quick.risks: The sources consulted do not discuss risks.
